settingText: Present-day temporary quarters aboard the exposed Vael-Tor dreadnought, repurposed by local authorities into a shelter and investigation site.
summary: After Adrian's revelation, Theo and Rae refuse to accept that they are the same people who lived through the war. Adrian offers no mystical proof; he tells them to revisit what they already remember.

dialogueInline.text: No. You don't get to say that and make it true.
Long enough that the question stopped helping.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Temporary living quarters improvised inside the exposed Vael-Tor dreadnought: cots, relief supplies, civilian partitions and work lamps bolted against ancient black hull. Theo, Rae and Adrian sit in a space made ordinary by necessity.

Panel 2 — Medium three-shot. Theo leans forward toward Adrian: 'No. You don't get to say that and make it true.' Rae stays back against the ancient hull, arms tight across herself, and asks, 'Same people for how long?' Adrian remains seated between their two lines of attack.
Panel 3 — Adrian: 'Long enough that the question stopped helping.' He does not offer chronology, mysticism or a technical explanation.
Panel 4 — Theo: 'Prove it.' Adrian: 'I can't.' Rae: 'Convenient.' Adrian stays seated, both hands open on his knees, and holds eye contact with Theo while Rae watches from the opposite side.

Panel 5 — Adrian: 'Remember it yourself.' Final wide image holds Theo and Rae on opposite sides of the cramped shelter, ancient black hull plating behind both of them and ordinary cots and relief supplies between them.

writingNotes.text: Keep Adrian from becoming a lore dispenser. He cannot demonstrate identity through a device or test. The only proof is recovered continuity, which he knows will hurt them.

settingText: Revisited ancient Desert Marker memory from Issue 1: same battlefield, same Starbreaker composition, but the frame is wider.
summary: Theo revisits the first Starbreaker memory. The exact composition from Issue 1 returns, then widens to reveal ancient Theo standing behind Mero with a satchel of dispatches. Mero addresses him naturally.

dialogueInline.text: You know what happens if I wait.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Reproduce the recognizable Issue 1 Desert Marker composition as closely as the production canon allows: Starbreaker confronting Mero, ancient battlefield and evacuation context, with the crop still excluding Theo. Starbreaker: 'You know what happens if I wait.'
Panel 2 — Repeat the composition but widen it one deliberate step. A shoulder, satchel strap and dispatch case appear behind Mero where the earlier memory had simply ended.

Panel 3 — Wider still: ancient Theo is fully visible behind Mero, younger in bearing but unmistakably the same person, dressed as a junior attaché with plain staff layers, dispatch satchel and worn papers. He stands naturally inside the command group.

Panel 4 — Mero turns only slightly: 'Theo.' Ancient Theo, already standing in the correct staff position behind him, answers without surprise, 'Sir.' Keep the exchange in a medium two-shot with the dispatch satchel and papers clearly visible.
Panel 5 — Mero: 'Stay close.' Theo automatically shifts half a step with him, tucks the dispatch case under one arm and falls into place at Mero's shoulder without hesitation.

writingNotes.text: Reproduce the key Issue 1 image deliberately so the reader recognizes it before the frame widens. Ancient Theo is not a ghost or modern observer; he belongs in the scene. He is younger in bearing but visibly the same person.

settingText: Present-day Vael-Tor shelter immediately after Theo returns from the revisited memory.
summary: Theo is shaken less by seeing himself than by the ordinary familiarity of Mero saying his name. Rae realizes recognition can restore relationship before it restores biography.

dialogueInline.text: I knew when he was about to ask me to stay.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Theo comes back into the same improvised shelter, unsteady but physically unharmed. Rae is beside him before Adrian can intervene.
Panel 2 — Theo: 'He knew my name.' He sits on the edge of the cot with both palms pressed against his knees, eyes wet and fixed on the floor; his breathing is shallow and he cannot look at Rae yet.
Panel 3 — Rae: 'You knew his voice.' Theo finally looks up at her. His expression changes abruptly and one hand lifts in the same attentive half-gesture ancient Theo used beside Mero.
Panel 4 — Theo: 'I knew when he was about to ask me to stay.' Show him unconsciously reproducing the same attentive posture ancient Theo took beside Mero.
Panel 5 — Rae: 'That's a memory.' Theo: 'I know.' End on recognition becoming autobiographical despite his resistance.

writingNotes.text: No spectacle. Theo is disturbed by intimacy: the cadence of Mero's voice, the expectation of a routine instruction, the feeling of having heard it many times.

settingText: Revisited ancient Pax-Aeterna memory from Issue 4: Arbiter at the black table after the extinction decision, frame extended to the previously unseen side.
summary: Rae revisits Arbiter's decision. The remembered frame widens and reveals ancient Rae seated beside Arbiter, writing the ruling. After the others leave, Arbiter asks whether Rae captured every word.

dialogueInline.text: Did you get all of it?
Even the part I crossed out?

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Repeat the established post-decision composition: Arbiter alone at the black Pax-Aeterna table after the others leave, same camera height, same chair placement, same light direction and same cropped empty space at frame right.
Panel 2 — Widen the frame to the previously unseen side of the table. A hand writing on a physical ruling sheet appears beside Arbiter.

Panel 3 — Wider reveal: ancient Rae sits beside Arbiter, visibly the same person in period-appropriate aide clothing, focused on the document as though this work is routine. She is not a ghost or observer from the present.

Panel 4 — Arbiter: 'Did you get all of it?' Rae: 'Yes.' Arbiter: 'Even the part I crossed out?' Insert on Rae's physical ruling sheet: the crossed-out line is visibly present but obscured by heavy ink and angle so its wording cannot be read.

Panel 5 — Rae: 'Especially that part.' Arbiter: 'Good.' End in a quiet two-shot with Rae continuing to write beside Arbiter, both seated close at the same table amid used pens, folded papers and the crossed-out ruling.

writingNotes.text: Ancient Rae is visibly the same person, not an ancestor. The shock comes from routine: she and Arbiter have done this kind of work together before. Preserve the crossed-out line as a future detail rather than revealing it yet.

settingText: Present-day dreadnought corridor overlooking Vael-Tor's modern city.
summary: Rae recognizes that she did not merely witness Arbiter's decisions; she helped preserve and frame them. She turns her anger on Adrian for allowing both of them to believe the visions were foreign.

dialogueInline.text: You let me call it someone else's history.
Because at first it was safer that way.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Present-day dreadnought corridor opened onto Vael-Tor city light through a temporary observation cut. Rae walks fast, angry; Theo and Adrian follow.
Panel 2 — Rae stops mid-corridor: 'I wrote it down.' Adrian: 'Yes.' Rae's pace breaks completely; she looks at her own writing hand and then closes it into a fist.
Panel 3 — Rae: 'You let me call it someone else's history.' Keep the exposed city and ancient hull in the same frame: nothing about this history is safely external anymore.
Panel 4 — Adrian: 'Because at first it was safer that way.' Theo immediately: 'For who?'
Panel 5 — Adrian: 'I don't know anymore.' End with Adrian physically isolated between Theo and Rae. His shoulders sag, his hands hang empty and he looks toward the floor instead of either of them.

writingNotes.text: Adrian's answer should weaken his moral certainty. He once believed concealment was protection; he can no longer say whom it protects.

settingText: Ancient aftermath of a devastated world, days after a major battle: shelters, wounded landscapes, survivors trying to rebuild ordinary life.
summary: Afterlight debuts among survivors, restoring what she can one person and place at a time. Atlas arrives expecting reassurance and finds her exhausted beyond anything he has seen before.

dialogueInline.text: They said you were finished here.
They say that whenever the fires stop.
I can give you an hour.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Ancient aftermath at human scale: shelters, patched roofs, burned streets, injured vegetation, survivors cooking and carrying water. Afterlight kneels beside one damaged living thing in the foreground while many other unfinished repairs remain visible across the settlement.
Panel 2 — Atlas arrives quietly and sees how exhausted she is. 'They said you were finished here.' Afterlight, without looking up: 'They say that whenever the fires stop.'

Panel 3 — Compose several needs in one frame around Afterlight: a wounded survivor waiting on a cot, a broken shelter roof, a dead patch of ground and a child carrying water. Afterlight can reach only the living plant immediately under her hands.
Panel 4 — Atlas: 'What do you need?' Afterlight looks up at him: 'For nothing else to happen.' Atlas's raised hand stops before touching her shoulder; both look out at the unfinished settlement.
Panel 5 — Atlas: 'I can give you an hour.' Afterlight: 'Then give me the hour.' End with Atlas turning outward to guard time while Afterlight returns to one small repair.

writingNotes.text: Afterlight's introduction must be intimate. She is not magically resetting a city. She is helping living things return where return is still possible, and she is tired. Atlas and Afterlight should feel like old allies who understand each other's burdens without speeches.

settingText: Same ancient aftermath later, at the edge of a district Afterlight could not restore.
summary: Starbreaker comes to see the aftermath of a battle he helped end. Afterlight refuses to let him use her restoration as proof that destruction can always be repaired.

dialogueInline.text: More than there would have been.
Turn what I can mend into permission for what you break.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Edge of a district where restoration simply stops. Behind Afterlight, some life and shelter have returned; ahead, the damage remains permanent. The boundary is irregular and human, not a glowing force line.
Panel 2 — Starbreaker arrives subdued, fractured armor dim. 'You saved it.' Afterlight: 'Part of it.' She looks toward what remains lost.
Panel 3 — Starbreaker: 'More than there would have been.' He means reassurance, not manipulation, which makes the mistake more painful.
Panel 4 — Afterlight: 'Don't do that.' Starbreaker: 'Do what?' Starbreaker genuinely pauses mid-step, brows drawn and open hands slightly raised; Afterlight turns fully toward him.

Panel 5 — Afterlight faces Starbreaker: 'Turn what I can mend into permission for what you break.' Leave a full body's width between them; the restored patch beside Afterlight and distant battle damage behind Starbreaker occupy opposite sides of the panel.

writingNotes.text: This should hurt like a relationship fracture, not an ideological debate. Afterlight has repaired Starbreaker's aftermath before. Starbreaker genuinely believed her existence made some of his choices survivable. She is withdrawing that comfort.

settingText: Present-day dreadnought records room where personal objects survived without understood provenance.
summary: Theo and Rae search physical remnants now that they know they belonged to this world. Theo finds Mero's old staff roster and his own name in it; Rae finds a handwriting sample she recognizes as hers before reading the signature.

dialogueInline.text: No. I mean I remember writing it like that.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Records room inside the exposed dreadnought: ordinary archival boxes, worn paper, personal effects and handwritten labels catalogued by present workers who never knew their provenance. No glowing data vault.
Panel 2 — Theo unfolds a damaged staff roster and finds his own name in a familiar hand: 'That's my name.' Rae: 'I know.'
Panel 3 — Theo traces the old letters with one fingertip: 'No. I mean I remember writing it like that.' Match his present hand position to the slant and spacing of the handwriting on the page.
Panel 4 — Rae has gone still over a different document before seeing its signature: 'So do I.' Theo looks across: 'Yours?'

Panel 5 — Rae turns the page far enough to reveal her own old signature near the bottom margin and says, 'Mine.' End on both of their hands resting beside the two recognizable handwriting samples on ordinary worn paper.

writingNotes.text: Physical proof should be ordinary and devastating: handwriting, worn paper, a familiar correction mark. No age dating. The objects do not prove how long ago the war was; they prove continuity of person.

settingText: Ancient restoration camp at night, Afterlight sitting among unfinished work while Atlas keeps watch.
summary: Afterlight admits to Atlas that she cannot keep pace with the destruction. It is not a cosmic theorem; it is an exhausted person saying there are now more places asking for help than she can reach.

dialogueInline.text: I used to arrive before the names were finished being read.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Night restoration camp. Occupied shelter beds, damaged plants, stacked names, repair materials and people sleeping in shifts surround Afterlight. Atlas sits on a low crate several feet away, keeping watch at her level.
Panel 2 — Afterlight: 'I used to arrive before the names were finished being read.' Hold on a simple memorial/list of names still growing while she sits exhausted.
Panel 3 — Atlas: 'You still arrive.' Afterlight: 'Not everywhere.' The distance between camps or need sites is suggested through departing messengers and requests she cannot follow.
Panel 4 — Atlas: 'No one can.' Afterlight: 'That's what I'm telling you.' Atlas starts to answer, then closes his mouth and looks across the rows of unfinished work instead.
Panel 5 — Close, quiet: Afterlight: 'I can't keep up.' Atlas has no answer. End on a person reaching her limit, not a cosmic law explained aloud.

writingNotes.text: Keep the established line 'I can't keep up' simple. Its power comes from cumulative human loss, not an explanation of entropy. Atlas understands what it means for the war: repair can no longer serve as everyone's moral excuse.

settingText: Present-day Vael-Tor overlook, modern city lights reflected across exposed ancient hull.
summary: Theo and Rae compare the roles they recovered. Both want to believe proximity to power was not participation. Neither can make that belief hold.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Present-day overlook above Vael-Tor, city lights reflected across the exposed dreadnought hull. Theo and Rae sit apart from the investigation activity below, finally alone with what they have learned.
Panel 2 — Theo: 'I carried messages.' Rae: 'I wrote things down.' Both reduce their ancient roles to the smallest possible description.
Panel 3 — Theo: 'That doesn't make us them.' Rae: 'No.' Her answer supports him verbally but not emotionally.
Panel 4 — Theo: 'You don't sound convinced.' He is really asking for permission not to feel responsible.
Panel 5 — Rae: 'Neither do you.' End with both looking at the ancient hull beneath the living city, unable to keep proximity and participation neatly separate.

writingNotes.text: Give them room to resist culpability. They should not instantly accept ancient selves as morally binding. The issue is about continuity arriving faster than self-forgiveness.

settingText: Ancient Mero staff room late at night during the war, quiet after senior commanders have left.
summary: Theo remembers a private routine with Mero. Mero asks the junior attaché what he thinks about a decision the senior staff could not resolve. The memory cuts before Theo can hear his own answer.

dialogueInline.text: Because you notice when the rest of us are.
What do you think we should do?

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Ancient staff room late at night after senior commanders have gone: abandoned cups, papers, worn chairs and one low practical light. Mero and ancient Theo remain working without ceremony.
Panel 2 — Mero: 'They're all very certain tonight.' Theo, sorting dispatches: 'That usually means they're scared.' His observation lands as familiar value, not insolence.
Panel 3 — Mero: 'That's why I kept you.' Theo looks up: 'Because I'm scared?' Theo gives a small crooked smile; one corner of Mero's mouth briefly lifts before he looks back toward the war-room door.

Panel 4 — Mero: 'Because you notice when the rest of us are.' Mero gives Theo the smallest tired smile and takes the dispatch from his hand; Theo remains beside him at the same shoulder position established in the earlier memory.

Panel 5 — Mero: 'What do you think we should do?' Ancient Theo begins to answer—but the panel cuts to white/black before any response is lettered or visually readable. The missing personal choice becomes the hook.

writingNotes.text: This is the first substantial ancient Theo scene. He is junior but not invisible to Mero. Cut the memory before his answer. The missing choice becomes the hook into the second half.

settingText: Present-day records room after both Theo and Rae are hit by incomplete personal memories.
summary: Theo remembers Mero asking for his opinion; Rae remembers starting to answer Arbiter after the extinction ruling. Neither can recover what they said. The next mystery becomes their own agency.

dialogueInline.text: He asked me what to do.
I don't know what I said.
You don't get to ask us not to remember anymore.

panelPlan.text: Panel 1 — Present-day records room. Theo returns from the cut-off memory abruptly; Rae is already shaken by a parallel incomplete recollection. Adrian finds them among ordinary papers and personal effects.
Panel 2 — Theo: 'He asked me what to do.' Rae: 'Arbiter asked me something too.' For the first time both memories place them near decision-making, not merely near history.
Panel 3 — Adrian: 'And?' Theo: 'I don't know what I said.' Rae: 'Neither do I.' The missing words are now the central threat.
Panel 4 — Adrian: 'Then don't rush it.' His old protective instinct returns automatically.

Panel 5 — Rae: 'You don't get to ask us not to remember anymore.' End with Rae reclaiming control of the investigation while Theo stands with her. The series question has changed to: what did I choose?

writingNotes.text: End on Rae taking control of the terms. Adrian can warn but no longer decide what truth they are allowed to have. The second-half question is now explicitly personal: what did I choose?
